name: Garden Sage
imageAlt: Illustration of garden sage with soft grey-green leaves
description: A hardy perennial with soft, silvery-green leaves and a warm, peppery, slightly piney flavor. Sage has been grown in kitchens and medicine gardens for centuries and its purple flowers are loved by bees.

growingConditions.watering: Moderate; let the soil dry out between waterings
growingConditions.soilType: Light, well-draining, neutral to slightly alkaline soil

uses: Fried in brown butter for pasta and gnocchi
Dried leaf tea and herbal gargles
Sage tea or a cooled infusion is a traditional gargle for sore throats and mouth irritation
Traditionally taken to ease mild indigestion and bloating
Folk remedy for excessive sweating and hot flashes
benefits: Contains rosmarinic acid and other antioxidants
Has natural antibacterial properties that help preserve food and freshen breath
Some small studies suggest sage extract may support memory and alertness
medicinal.caution: Common sage contains thujone, so enjoy it in cooking and tea amounts only. Avoid medicinal doses and the essential oil during pregnancy or if you have epilepsy.

video.title: Sage Growing Guide: Plant, Care, Prune, Harvest & Dry

taste: Earthy, peppery and slightly minty, with a warm, savory depth.
sideEffects: Common sage contains thujone, which can be harmful in large amounts or over a long time
Large doses can cause restlessness, dizziness or, rarely, seizures
The essential oil is strong and should not be swallowed

safety.allergy: Sage is a mint-family plant, so allergic reactions are possible in people sensitive to similar herbs.
safety.pregnancy: Avoid medicinal amounts and sage oil during pregnancy. Food amounts are generally fine.
safety.pets: Sage is generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but the essential oil is not safe for them.
safety.medications: Sage may affect blood sugar medicines and anti-seizure medicines. People with epilepsy should avoid medicinal doses.

temperature: Hardy and tough. Common sage survives winter cold of about -20 °C and copes with summer heat. It grows best at about 15-30 °C.
harvest: Pick leaves whenever the plant is established, but take only a little in the first year. The flavor is best before the plant flowers. Never take more than a third at once, and cut stems back just above a leaf pair.
storage: Wrap fresh leaves in a damp paper towel in the fridge for about a week. Hang small bunches to dry in a warm, airy place, or freeze whole leaves.
dailyLife: Fry leaves in brown butter for pasta and gnocchi
Add to stuffing, sausages and roast pork
Use a cooled infusion as a gargle for a sore throat
Brew a leaf or two as a tea
tips: Cut back by about a third each spring to keep it from getting woody
Choose a sunny spot with sharp drainage
Replace plants every few years, because old ones get leggy

origin.details: Common sage is native to the northern Mediterranean, especially the Balkan coast. Its Latin name comes from a word meaning to heal.
